title: Third Homily on the Day of the Dormition

sections.heading: The final mystery presupposes earlier mysteries

pairs.en: Blessing today the Dormition of the Mother of God, the Holy Church calls this falling asleep “the final mystery accomplished in her.” Since a final, or concluding, mystery necessarily presupposes mysteries that came before it, from the very beginning, the question has probably occurred to more than one hearer of the Church's hymns: what are these mysteries? It is our duty to give an answer; and we are all the more glad to do so because a consideration of the mysteries wrought upon the Mother of God in the course of her life can, on the one hand, serve to glorify her on this present day of “the final mystery accomplished in her,” and on the other, can be a rich source of edifying reflection and consoling feeling. One thing alone might give us pause: every mystery loves to remain untouched and does not suffer cold inquiry. But we shall touch the mysteries in the life of the Mother of God not with dry questions and cold puzzlement, but with faith and love for her all-honoured memory.

The first mystery in the life of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary was revealed with her coming into the world. For of whom was she born? Of aged parents, as holy tradition tells us — as the fruit of special prayer and a vow. The Wisdom of God willed that she who was to give birth without knowing wedlock should herself be the fruit not so much of the powers of nature as of the visitation of grace. And so Joachim and Anna reach those years in which all hope of becoming father or mother is lost. But this holy pair possess a faith that conquers the laws of nature; and through this faith, accompanied by fervent prayer, Mary appears — a pure gift of heaven, and for that very reason able to be an unfailing source of blessings for the earth. Thus was accomplished the first mystery, the birth of the Most Blessed one.

sections.heading: The second mystery: the temple and the Holy of Holies

pairs.en: The second mystery came upon her at her entry into the temple, at three years of age. That entry at such an age was in itself extraordinary — the consequence of a special, exceptional vow: to dedicate the fruit of their prayers to the Lord. And by this entry into the temple, the future Mother of the Son of God was given the possibility of being raised at the temple, and so of becoming kindred in spirit and heart, from her earliest years, with everything holy. Yet even living at the temple, the Daughter of Joachim, in the ordinary course of things, should have remained in its forecourt. Instead, as tradition testifies, she was given permission by the high priests to pass within the veil, to enter the Holy of Holies — where only the great high priest alone had the right to enter, once a year. We do not know for certain in consequence of what extraordinary events or revelations she received this exceptional and unexampled privilege; but we see at once that this mystery of entering the Holy of Holies was supremely fitting for the future Mother of the Son of God. It was proper that the living Ark of God should appear, at least from time to time, in the place where its symbol and prefiguration — the ark of the covenant with the manna and the tablets — had once been kept continually.

sections.heading: The third mystery: virginity joined to betrothal

pairs.en: The third mystery followed when the Holy Virgin came of age. The Old Testament, as is well known, knew no state of virginity dedicated to God and sanctified by the law. Therefore, when the Daughter of Joachim and Anna reached full age at the temple of Jerusalem, the high priests wished to send her away from the temple so that, after the example of the other maidens of Israel, she might choose herself a husband. But the Holy Virgin firmly declared that she had resolved, for her whole life, to belong to no one but God alone. The high priests did not know what to do; and after deliberations and prayers, they resolved to betroth her to a man who would agree to bear the name of husband without exercising a husband's rights. The lot fell to the elder Joseph; and so Mary becomes a wife without ceasing to be a virgin, and thus unites in herself virginity and marriage, the blessing of the Old Covenant and the grace of the New. And meanwhile this mystery of betrothal, this marriage in name, serves for a time as the covering necessary for the great mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God, shielding the Holy Virgin from all suspicion — both on the part of the Jews, who otherwise would not have been slow to count her a criminal, and on the part of that ancient enemy who, awaiting the Seed of the woman that was to crush his head, would have thrown heaven and earth into turmoil had he seen that a Virgin who knew no wedlock had conceived a Son in her womb.

How the most glorious mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God itself was accomplished is known to each and every one from the Gospel. The Archangel brought the good tidings; the Virgin said humbly, *Behold the handmaid of the Lord* (Luke 1:38); the power of the Most High overshadowed her — and the Word became flesh! (John 1:14). This is the summit of the mysteries accomplished in the Most Holy Virgin. But this summit of mysteries was not their end. No — the mysteries continued; only they went deeper, became less visible, without ceasing to be instructive and consoling. Do you wish to know what these mysteries were?

sections.heading: The mystery of the Mother's crucifixion

pairs.en: First, the mystery of crucifixion. Whose? The Son's? No — the Mother's. Yes, my brethren: on the cross there was not the Son alone; the Mother was there too. When? Throughout her whole life, but especially on Golgotha. For did not the Divine Son Himself say: *he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after Me, is not worthy of Me!* (Matthew 10:38). And who could be more worthy of the Son than His Mother? Therefore no one, ever, has borne such a cross through the course of a life as the Most Blessed Virgin Mary. This cross was fashioned not of wood or of any material, but of the greatness befitting the Mother of God — and of the humiliation in which this Mother remained until her very death. Consider: the Archangel himself calls her full of grace and summons her to joy; she is already carrying the Son of God in her womb; and at the same time she must suffer suspicion before the guardian of her virginity — and what suspicion! That she has betrayed her betrothal!.. Is that not a cross? The time draws near for her to give birth to Him whose Kingdom shall have no end — and there is no room for her in the inns of Bethlehem; she must bear Him in a cave and lay Him in a manger!.. Is that not a cross?.. Angels sing, “Glory to God in the highest”; magi bow down and bring gifts — and immediately after this, fleeing from Herod, she must escape by night into Egypt, along a road scarcely passable even by day! Is that not a cross? And on Golgotha — what, do you think, did the Mother's heart feel when the Son cried out in His agony: *My God, My God... why hast Thou forsaken Me!* (Psalm 22:1). Here, beyond all doubt, Simeon's dreadful prophecy was fulfilled in all its force: *Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also!* (Luke 2:35). And when the sword had pierced the very soul, there was no need to pierce the hands and feet: the mystery of spiritual crucifixion was accomplished!..

sections.heading: After Golgotha: the mystery of adoption to John

pairs.en: With the completion of this mystery, it might have seemed that everything of the grave would now be taken away from the Mother, as it had been taken away from the Son — that after the resurrection she would begin to shine visibly before the whole world with the glory of the Risen One. On the contrary: to the end of her life Mary remains in obscurity, in the humblest of lots. Why so? Because upon the mystery of her co-crucifixion with the Son on Golgotha there followed at once another mystery — her adoption to John: a mystery noticed by few, but no less astonishing, and rich in spiritual instruction.

Indeed, brethren, have you ever reflected on this wondrous adoption that took place on Golgotha? Have you entered into the purpose and spirit of this act? Why is the Mother of the Son of God here given as Mother to the disciple, and thus, as it were, brought down for a time from the height of her unexampled greatness? Was it really so that she might have shelter in John's house? But who among the believers, after the Son's resurrection, could have refused refuge to His Mother?.. And is it from the cross that such earthly, minor arrangements would be made? No: the mysterious words, *Woman, behold thy son!* (John 19:26) have a deeper meaning. By them the character of the whole remainder of the Mother of God's life is determined; here is the key to the explanation of everything that afterwards happened to her. Attend!

sections.heading: Why glory was withheld from her on earth

pairs.en: When the Godhead of the Son, with His resurrection and ascension into heaven, was revealed in all its power — when the whole world began to bow before the name of the Crucified — then, naturally, the greatest honour and glory awaited the Mother of Jesus, the honour befitting the Mother of the Son of God, the Saviour of mankind. No one, without question, could have been more worthy of this honour and glory than Mary; and no one, without question, would have used them so holily and in so godly a manner as the Most Blessed Virgin. But glory during her earthly life — besides depriving her of the closest likeness to her Divine Son, who to the end of His life had nowhere to lay His head — would have carried with it this weighty disadvantage: the enemies of Christianity would not have failed, in that case, to find in her the person of its Founder's kin and turn it into a reproach against the progress of the Gospel. The great and miraculous work of turning the whole world to God would not have been free of ties and relations which, however perfectly pure, were still earthly and human; and the very preachers of the Gospel would have found it difficult to place themselves in a proper relation to the glorified Mother of Him whose manger and cross they preached. And behold: by the adoption of the Most Holy Virgin to John on Golgotha, all these difficulties are removed. At the very summit of spiritual greatness, at the very moment of the greatest sacrifice — the moment from which Mary's glory should have begun — she is, by the mysterious words *behold thy son!*, brought down, as it were, into the circle of ordinary mothers; by her adoption to John she is pointed, for all the rest of her life, to the simple lot of the first Christian woman.

sections.heading: Her lifelong hiddenness — the Scriptures' eloquent silence

pairs.en: And see how deeply the Handmaid of the Lord understood this mystery of adoption! How faithful she remains, all her life, to the direction given from the Cross! For what do we see in the rest of that life? A resolute withdrawal from every kind of glory, amid all the miraculous spread of Christianity. The book of the Acts of the Holy Apostles tells in detail of the establishment of the first Christian churches; it records the deeds of the chief apostles; it presents the various conversions of Jews and pagans to Christ — but Mary you do not see. Only once, and that in passing, is it mentioned that she was with the disciples in the upper room of Zion on the day of Pentecost. (For how could she not be present at the descent of the Spirit — she who had conceived and given birth by the Spirit?) But after that, not a word about all the rest of her life; not a word about her very death. Say yourselves: is this silence not a mystery? And what does it mean, if not this — that Mary, by removing herself from every form of glory, showed a new proof of humility, the deepest humility, and so became still more worthy of that crown of glory which had long belonged to her by every right?

sections.heading: The crown descends at her Dormition

pairs.en: But sooner or later this crown had at last to descend upon the head of her who is more honourable than the Cherubim and the Seraphim — and descend it did, at the time of her Dormition. Yet a life filled with mysteries did not remain without mystery even here. What would have been surprising in the Mother of the Son of God being taken up into heaven without tasting death? Did not simple fittingness, in a certain way, even demand it, when Enoch and Elijah had already been granted that high lot? But another destiny was appointed for Mary. As if for the comfort and reassurance of all of us who must pass through the gates of death, the Mother of God also dies, and so shares the debt of nature with all the earthborn. But as the Mother of the Son of God — of Him who said of Himself, *I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in Me, though he were dead, yet shall he live* (John 11:25) — Mary, like her Divine Son, is not held by the bonds of death. Even in the tomb her body does not see corruption, and after three days it is taken up, ensouled once more, with glory into heaven. From that time all the veils are removed; the living Tabernacle of God appears in all her beauty; the most holy Ark of the New Covenant is set in its place; she who is more honourable than the Cherubim is exalted above all the heavens; and the whole universe begins to bless her who has become a source of blessings for the entire human race.

sections.heading: Wondrous are your mysteries, O Theotokos

pairs.en: Contemplating such mysteries in the life of the Most Blessed Virgin — and we have pointed out only the chief of them — who will not cry out to her joyfully today, together with the Church: “Wondrous are Thy mysteries, O Theotokos!” Wondrous in thy grace-filled conception and birth; wondrous in thy marvellous entry into the temple, and thy still more marvellous entering into the Holy of Holies; wondrous in thy unexampled betrothal to the holy Joseph, bearing the name of wife without knowing a husband; wondrous in thy seedless conceiving and bearing, of the Holy Spirit, of the Eternal Son of God; wondrous in thy unceasing sufferings after the example of thy Son and God, and thy endurance of many and various crosses and temptations; wondrous in thy mysterious adoption to John, and thy renunciation of all earthly glory; wondrous, finally, in thy very Dormition, and in the taking up of thy Most Pure Body afterwards, with glory, into heaven!

sections.heading: Our own lives are not without mysteries

pairs.en: But, my brethren, while we marvel with reverence at the holy mysteries of God's Providence in the life of the Most Blessed Virgin, and in godly fashion bless the memory of her Dormition today by contemplating them, let us not forget that our life, too, is not without mysteries — that these mysteries of our life resemble the mysteries in the life of the Mother of God, who is the pattern of all our lives. Above all, let us not forget that some of the mysteries of our life are accomplished upon us without us, while others — and precisely the most important, on which our eternal destiny depends — absolutely require our participation, and, remaining unaccomplished in us for lack of it, can bring us under dreadful condemnation.

Which mysteries of God's Providence are accomplished upon us without us and without our participation? Chiefly two: the mystery of our entry into this world and the mystery of our departure from it — that is, the mystery of our birth and of our death. Who has ever determined his own coming into the world? No one. And who can determine his own end? Again, no one. Both the one and the other are in the hands of God; and since they are in the hands of God, we can be at peace regarding these mysteries of our life, firmly believing that the almighty power and wisdom of God have done, and will do — if we surrender ourselves to God's will — everything for us and on our behalf that is needful and profitable for us, and will do it more successfully than we, left to ourselves, could ever have done.

sections.heading: The mysteries that require our consent

pairs.en: But there are other mysteries — and, as I have said, the most important ones — which, though they absolutely must be accomplished in us during our life for the sake of our eternal happiness, cannot be accomplished in us without us, without our free choice and cooperation. These are the mystery of the grace-filled indwelling of the Lord Jesus in us, and the mystery of our co-crucifixion with Him in spirit and in truth. For why did the Son of God leave heaven and, taking up His dwelling in the womb of the Most Blessed Virgin, appear as a Man like ourselves? So that, having accomplished the work of our redemption, having freed us by His death from sin and the curse, He might then come to dwell by His grace in each one who believes in His name — dwell in us so that we might be one spirit with Him, as it were one person. Without this mysterious indwelling of His in us, and our union with Him, the mystery of our salvation cannot be accomplished in us; and we, for all our participation in the Christian faith and even in its Sacraments, will one day be found strangers to Christ and to the Kingdom of Heaven which He purchased for us. But the mystery of our union with our Saviour cannot be accomplished without a prior cleansing of our sinful and impure nature; without our dying to sin and sensuality; without the denial of a will corrupted by self-love and the passions — in short, without our co-crucifixion with Him in our spirit and heart. And who can do all this in us without us? Plainly, no one. If we do not resolve to die to sin, so as to come alive with Christ in a new life of grace, we shall remain alive to the world but dead to God. If we remain dead to God and to a righteous life, then our Saviour, as the Most Holy of the holy, will not come to dwell in us, unclean and unrepentant as we are, and will not become in us the beginning and source of eternal life; and without this, serving the world and slaving all our life for the flesh, we shall die in our sins and be cast out from the face of God.

Therefore, seeing how these great mysteries were accomplished in the Mother of God herself — how by purity of life and by humility she attained the grace of becoming the vessel of the Son of God according to the flesh, and how she then nourished and preserved that grace by labours of pure love and self-denial — let us turn our attention to our own life and conduct, to see whether there is in us even the beginning of these mysteries: whether we strive for our grace-filled drawing near in spirit to our Saviour, for mysterious union with Him with our whole being; and whether, to that end, we are gradually cleansing ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, enclosing our will more and more within His most holy will, loving His Cross, and bearing with good heart the trials He sends upon us for our purification and to draw us to Himself. Blessed is he who has long been acquainted with these great and holy mysteries and sees them being accomplished in himself! For such a one it remains only to press on and stay faithful to the end. Blessed, too, is he who came to know the importance of these mysteries late, but, having come to know it, lost no time in doing everything so that they might begin to be accomplished in him as well! But what will become of the man who gives no thought at all to his salvation or to his Saviour? For him also the time of the last mystery of life will come — the time of death; and how terrible that mystery will be for him, in itself, and still more in its consequences! For if even the death of the sinner, by the testimony of the word of God, is grievous, the immortality of sinners is more grievous and more terrible still. Amen.
